readerTitle: Why a rate rise hits the warehouse harder than the forklift
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류 회사, 소프트웨어 회사) + 실제 관찰 (2022~2023년 미국 금리 인상기의 성장주 하락). 계산 수치는 설명용
insight: 금리는 빌린 돈의 비용이 아니라 시간의 가격이다. 금리가 오르면 수익이 먼 미래에 들어오는 사업일수록 오늘의 가치가 크게 줄어든다.
misconception: 빚이 없으면 금리가 올라도 우리 사업과는 상관없다. 금리 인상은 모든 투자에 똑같이 영향을 준다.

sources.text: Federal Reserve, FOMC statements, March 2022 to July 2023 (federal funds target range)
물류 회사·소프트웨어 회사 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 미 연준 기준금리 목표 범위: 2022년 3월 인상 전 0~0.25%, 2023년 7월 5.25~5.50%. 카드에는 'near zero'와 'above 5%'로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 FOMC 자료로 재확인하세요.
'아직 이익을 내지 못하는 고성장 소프트웨어 기업의 주가가 2022년 시장 전체보다 훨씬 크게 떨어졌다'는 일반적 관찰로만 적었습니다. 특정 기업명이나 하락률은 쓰지 않았습니다. 지수 비교 자료(예: 고성장 소프트웨어 지수 vs S&P 500)로 방향성을 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why a rate rise hits the warehouse harder than the forklift
body: A logistics company has no loans. Then interest rates rise from 2% to 6%.
Its forklift upgrade barely notices. But the money its new warehouse will earn ten years from now just became worth about a third less today.

image.label: A small forklift and a large warehouse on a seesaw tilted by a rising percent sign
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 시소 한쪽에 작은 지게차, 다른 쪽에 큰 창고. 가운데 받침대 위에 '%' 기호가 위로 올라가며 창고 쪽이 크게 내려앉음. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Rates just went up. You pay cash.
body: You run a regional logistics firm. You plan two projects, both paid from your own cash. One is a sorting machine that pays for itself within a year. The other is a new warehouse whose payoff arrives mostly in years five to ten.
Rates rise from 2% to 6%. What happens to these plans?

options.text: Nothing. We aren't borrowing, so rates don't matter
options.feedback: You avoid loan costs, but your cash now has a better use: it could earn 6% elsewhere. Every project must now beat that.

options.text: Both look a bit worse, by about the same amount
options.feedback: Right that both are affected. But the size of the hit depends on how long you wait for the money.

options.text: The warehouse takes a much bigger hit
options.feedback: Yes. The further away the payoff, the more a higher rate shrinks it. The next card shows how much.

cards.title: What $100 in the future is worth today
body: Money due in one year loses about 4% of its value today when rates go from 2% to 6%. Money due in ten years loses about **a third**.

cards.title: Interest rates
body: An **interest rate** is the price of money over time. It's what a lender charges for waiting to be paid back, and what your own cash could earn if you simply set it aside.
That second part is why rates matter even without debt. If safe savings pay 6%, a project that earns 5% is a worse deal than doing nothing. A higher rate raises the bar every plan has to clear.

image.label: A price tag hanging on an hourglass
image.brief: 모래시계에 가격표가 달려 있고 가격표에 '%' 표시. 배경은 단순한 단색. 메시지: 금리는 시간의 가격. 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Waiting is charged again every year.
body: Money due next year is discounted once. Money due in ten years is discounted ten times over, because the rate compounds.
At 2%, ten years of waiting adds up to about 22%. At 6%, it adds up to about 79%. So a four-point rise barely touches next year's cash but cuts deep into cash a decade away.
That's the twist: the same rate change does not hit every plan equally. **Time to payoff** decides the damage.

cards.title: When rates rose, distant profits got cheaper.
body: In 2022 and 2023, the US Federal Reserve raised its main rate from near zero to above 5%.

Many fast-growing software companies that had not yet made a profit saw their share prices fall far more than the overall market. Investors were buying profits expected years away, and those were exactly the profits a higher rate shrinks most.
Steady businesses with cash coming in today felt the change less.

image.label: Two lines: a steady business dips slightly, a future-profit business drops sharply
image.brief: 단순한 선 그래프 두 개(실제 데이터 아님, 개념도). 'Cash today' 선은 살짝 내려가고 'Profits far in the future' 선은 크게 떨어짐. 배경에 위로 오르는 '%' 계단. 기업명·로고 없음, 'Illustration' 표기.

cards.title: Don't just kill every long project.
body: A strong long-term project can still clear a higher bar. The point is to test it against today's rate, not to stop investing.
The rate that matters is your own. Small businesses usually borrow above the headline rate, and the rate you can earn on spare cash may be lower.
Rates also move with inflation. A 6% rate when prices rise 5% a year is not as tight as it sounds.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your software company has no debt and plenty of cash. You planned a three-year platform rebuild that should start paying off in year four. Rates have just risen sharply, and investors are asking about profits.
What do you do with the rebuild?

options.text: Keep it exactly as planned. We have no debt
options.feedback: You keep the long-term vision, but you ignore that your cash now earns more elsewhere and that payoffs in year four are worth much less today.

options.text: Split it into stages that each ship value sooner, and require a bigger payoff
options.feedback: Earlier payoffs lose less to a higher rate, and you can stop after any stage. You give up some design freedom for less risk.

options.text: Pause all long-term work until rates fall
options.feedback: It protects cash now, but rates can stay high for years, and a rival who keeps building may pull ahead.

cards.title: Interest rates are the price of waiting.
body: When rates rise, money far in the future is worth less today, whether or not you borrow. The longer the wait, the bigger the hit.
**Try it today:** list your three biggest planned investments. Next to each, write how many years until it pays back. Ask which one would still make sense if rates rose two points.
